Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-52 Filed 03/02/26 Page 404 of 429 Stauffer Chemical (Houston, TX): In 1989, a number of chemical plants along the Houston ship channel had releases of hydrogen sulfide on a number of occasions. Due to the odors associated with this chemical, the local community had significant concern about the possible health effects of the emissions. Stauffer had installed a number of preventive measures as well as on-line continuous monitors for this chemical. Our job was to attend the public meetings wherein the renewal of their operating permit was discussed. As such, we needed to explain a number of scientific issues to a relatively hostile audience. City of Detroit (world’s largest municipal incinerator): In 1991, Mayor Coleman Young of Detroit had run into significant difficulty in maintaining the permits to operate Detroit’s municipal incinerators. For a number of years, the Canadian government had expressed concern about the release of airborne chemicals by these incinerators and the drift of the plume toward the Canadian border. Due to dozens of questions which had been raised about the possibility that dioxins were being admitted from the incinerators, Mayor Young and the operators of the incinerators, wanted us to give presentations to the air pollution control district at their next public meeting and to answer the public’s questions. I developed some teaching materials for that meeting and answered several hours of questions from the community (in early 1992). Nearly 500 people attended that meeting. GSF Industries (Calumet City, IN): As a result of an accidental release of a scrubbing agent (selexol) from a gas recycling exhaust system, a number of cars besides this landfill had had their paint pitted. Because nearly 100 autos had been affected, local residents believed that it was likely that the particulate released during the accident would affect their health. Our client asked that we conduct a screening risk assessment and present our findings to residents in the area. In 1990, a public question/answer session took place in a largely poor-minority neighborhood outside Chicago for about 2.5 hours. Syntex Agribusiness and Region VII USEPA (Springfield, MO): In 1978, dioxin contaminated oils were used as dust control for a number of towns in central Missouri. Most famous among these was Times Beach, Missouri. Although this site received most of the press coverage, a good deal of remediation activities was required at the two manufacturing sites from which the oils originated or were analyzed. As a result of those activities, USEPA and Syntex Agribusiness wanted to conduct remediation activities at both the Verona and the Springfield sites. Because the townspeople had read literally hundreds of pages of information on dioxin for nearly 15 years, they were quite nervous about living near a remediation activity involving this chemical. At the request of the Region VII Administrator (Mr. Morris Kay), a public hearing was conducted in 1989 to explain the risks to humans and the environmental associated with the upcoming remediation activities. Fortunately, as a result of that meeting, the remediation process began to occur without significant resistance from either the community or local environmental action groups. 970 W Broadway Ave, Suite E-395 Jackson, WY 83001 TRCcompanies.com Tel: 415.509.4085 Email: DPaustenbach@trccompanies.com

SUMMARY OF GENERAL OPINIONS RELATED TO KRATOM SAFETY, USE, ADDICTIVENESS AND REGULATORY STATUS IN THE UNITED STATES 21. In this section I provide my foundational opinions and facts related to kratom science, public health context, and regulatory framework. These pertain to the broad universe of kratom products available and marketed in the United States, recognizing that products vary widely in their purity, efforts to assure that they are not adulterated, their alkaloid contents and 4

In contrast, the OPMS products alleged to have been consumed by Harmony Moller and to have caused her death are made to higher standards and compliant with the American Kratom Association’s Good Manufacturing Practice (“GMP”) Standards Program. Opinion 1: 22. Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the United States Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) or under the International Drug Control Conventions of United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“DHHS”), DEA and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (“UNODC”) that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. Opinion 2: 23. Kratom is not characterized by “high abuse,” “dependence” or “addiction” potential and is well within the range of many licit consumer dietary substances and health products (e.g., caffeine, antihistamines, and CBD) that are abused and can be addictive in some people but overall are used primarily for their beneficial and otherwise useful health and/or life-enhancing effects. Opinion 3: 24. Kratom does not carry a high risk of death. To the contrary, the risk of death by kratom alone appears very low and rare. This has also been the conclusion of NIDA and DEA for approximately a decade and similarly concluded by FDA in 2024 after its approximately decade of review and own testing. My opinion continues to be consistent with Assistant Secretary Gior’s 2018 review statement on this matter: “There is still debate among reputable scientists over whether kratom by itself is associated with fatal overdoses.” Opinion 4: 25. There is no consensus on the basis by which kratom might cause life threatening effects or death; in contrast to most substances that contribute to overdose deaths (e.g., respiratory depression by opioids and sedatives, cardiovascular incidents by stimulants). Opinion 5: 26. There is no consensus on what level of kratom consumption or level in the bloodstream would constitute a lethal dose, in contrast to most substances of high abuse, addiction and mortality potential that contribute to the U.S. drug overdose epidemic. Specifically, there is no well-defined toxidrome for kratom, but rather kratom associated deaths most commonly involve other substances, including prescription and non-prescribed drugs, and various pre-existing disease conditions. Deaths occurring in the absence of use of other substances are rare, as concluded by NIDA (2022) and FDA (2024). Opinion 6: 5

Kratom is an overall public health asset that is used by many people as a harm reduction approach to reduce or eliminate the use of opioids, sedatives, stimulants, and alcohol. Such public health benefits were considered in the determinations of the DEA, the DHHS, and the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence not to schedule kratom as a controlled substance. Opinion 7: 28. Most people use kratom for health and well-being, including as a supplement to, or replacement for, caffeinated beverages or to self-manage depression, anxiety, pain, or opioid and other drug withdrawal. Like many dietary substances that consumers use, the health and well- being benefits of kratom are not and cannot be approved for therapeutic use by the FDA. Opinion 8: 29. Kratom is a legally marketed product in 44 states, and it is legal for people in those states to possess and consume kratom. Moreover, at the time of this writing, the legislatures of 18 states have passed laws to ensure legal access to kratom with varying approaches to ensure that products meet their standards for safe access and potential benefit to public health and adults who choose to consume kratom. Opinion 9: 30. Kratom carries a low risk of producing a medical condition requiring treatment, such as Substance Use Disorder (“SUD,” also known as “dependency” or “addiction”) or withdrawal disorder (also referred to as “physical” or “physiological” dependence). However, mild to moderate SUD and/or withdrawal following discontinuation of kratom use is not uncommon in people who consume kratom repeatedly every day for at least several months. In contrast with opioid, alcohol, and stimulant use and withdrawal disorders for which treatment is often sought, most kratom users who reported dependence or addiction did not seek treatment and found it self-manageable and not debilitating. Opinion 10: 31. The vast majority of the evidence upon which I base my opinions was generated by independent researchers primarily supported by the National Institutes of Health (“NIH”) and NIDA and not commercial kratom product developers or kratom advocacy organizations such as the American Kratom Association. Such studies have been published at an increasing rate over the past decade at leading biomedical research institutions, including Johns Hopkins, the University of Florida, the NIDA intramural program itself and many others. Only a few percent of such publications were supported by commercial companies or foundations. Opinion 11: 32. OPINIONS SPECIFIC TO PLAINTIFFS’ CLAIMS 35. In this section I provide opinions specific to Plaintiff’s allegations. 36. Plaintiff has not provided valid and reliable support for the allegation that kratom was the cause, or a substantial contributing factor, to Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023. 37. The coroner’s report, as cited in the Complaint (para 33), suggests potential pre- existing heart abnormalities, e.g., “Abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff.” The coroner’s report does not provide a basis for concluding that mitragynine contributed to Ms. Moller’s death. I note that blood levels of mitragynine were far lower than those that are sometimes associated with death (150 ng/mL by NMS Labs and 158 ng/mL by UC). NMS labs did not find a positive result for the mitragynine metabolite, 7-hydroxymitragynine (“7-OH”), which is consistent with low kratom/mitragynine intake. However, the NMS Labs reports did identify several other pharmacological substances and metabolites. 38. Although I do not have an opinion on the actual cause of Ms. Moller’s death, my scientific training and experience make clear that singling out kratom use as the primary or substantial contributor to death is confounded by Ms. Moller’s potential preexisting conditions and other substance use. 39. The autopsy finding that Ms. Moller’s pre-existing heart condition was “exacerbated by Mitragynine use” is speculative. There is no established scientific or medical consensus that mitragynine “exacerbates” Ms. Moller’s specific and rare cardiac anomaly or causes death in such circumstances. This is distinct from substances with well-defined mechanisms of lethal toxicity (e.g., respiratory depression from classic opioids or hypertensive crisis from classic stimulants). As Eckhardt and Nickel (2023) have concluded, “Some case reports of kratom associated arrhythmia, including fatalities, have surfaced, but little is known of the mechanism of kratom-induced ventricular arrythmia nor the depth of the problem.” 40. Attributing causation to mitragynine is confounded by (a) Ms. Moller’s pre-existing cardiac condition noted in the coroner’s report, (b) the multiple empty liquor and prescription pill bottles (including Acyclovir, methylphenidate, hydrocodone/acetaminophen, and gabapentin) and drug paraphernalia found at the scene (see St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office Incident Report), 7

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-53 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 199 and (c) the toxicology report confirming the presence of multiple other drugs and substances such as diphenhydramine, promethazine, and marijuana (THC finding). Note that evidence of marijuana use is of concern because my own marijuana research and many others have found that marijuana can produce rapid and pronounced tachycardia (Heishman et al. 1990; Huestis et al. 1992) arrythmias and ventricular fibrillation (see also .NIDA, 2024; Paulraj, 2024. Furthermore as found in my own research (Heishman et al . 1990 and Huestis et al. 1992) plasma THC levels plummet rapidly beginning with minutes following the marijuana vapor/smoke inhalation which means that seemingly low levels of THC exposure from post mortem blood samples can greatly underestimate actual exposure (see also NEW REF COMING). 41. I do not see any basis in the autopsy report or NMS labs assessment of mitragynine or 7-OH levels that suggest anything but relatively low levels as compared to those that are more likely to be associated with death (see Papsun et al. 2023; Henningfield, Grundmann, Huestis and Smith, 2026). The mitragynine level was determined to be 150 ng/mL by NMS Labs and 158 ng/mL by UCSF Clinical Toxicology. NMS did not report 7-OH. UCSF Clinical Toxicology reported 0.8 ng/mL with a footnote indicating the “[v]alue was below the lower limit of quantification of 3 ng/mL and equal to the limit of detection for the analysis.” 42. Huestis et al, 2024 assessed the effects of single and consecutive daily oral ascending doses of dried kratom leaf powder in healthy adults, including the mitragynine and 7- OH concentrations, over 10 days after a single dose and 23 days after multiple dosing. This was a Health Canada approved study designed to detect kratom-related adverse effects. In the trial’s highest dose group (4000mg kratom leaf powder / 53.2mg mitragynine daily for 15 days), the mean steady state peak plasma concentration (Cmax) measured was 143 ng/mL with a median of 155 ng/mL (range 64.3 – 215 ng/mL). In this same group, the mean 7-OH level measured was 21- 8 ng/mL (range 13.3 – 31.7 ng/mL). The study concluded that the kratom powder was well- tolerated with no clinically significant abnormal findings in blood pressure, heart rate, or ECG. No active participants had abnormal QTc intervals, and QTc intervals greater than 500 milliseconds were not reported. 43. Reissig et al., 2024 evaluated the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and safety of single ascending oral doses of botanical kratom in non-dependent, recreational polydrug users with opioid experience. In this pilot, placebo-controlled, dose-finding study performed under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application, participants were administered single doses of 1g, 3g, 8g, 10g, or 12g of oral kratom powder in capsules. In the highest dose groups, Cmax for mitragynine ranged from 250-300 ng/mL but 7-OH levels were below the lower limit of quantitation. The study concluded that at the doses tested, kratom was well-tolerated with no serious adverse effects reported, including no abnormalities in vital signs and ECG. 44. Smith et al., 2024 assessed the acute effects of a “typical” morning dose of kratom in 10 adults who use kratom regularly. This was an observational study designed to measure physiological, subjective, and psychomotor effects and to quantify alkaloids in plasma. Participants self-administered their typical dose of kratom (mean 5.16 g, range 1.1-10.9g). The mean plasma concentration for mitragynine found was 175.6 ng/mL (median 174.5 ng/mL, range 36.6 – 396.5 ng/mL). The mean plasma concentration for 7-OH was 34.0 ng/mL (median 27.4 ng/mL, range 2.9 – 77.7 ng/mL). The study concluded that among these regular consumers, there were “few clinically significant differences” pre- and post-dosing. Physiological changes, 8

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-53 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 199 including those in blood pressure and heart rate, were described as “minor” and “not clinically significant.” 45. Each of these studies recorded mitragynine blood concentrations at levels similar or higher than what was found in this case. 46. Taken together, these data from clinical studies, designed to the standards of an FDA registration study for safety (Huestis et al. 2024 and Reissig et al. 2024) observed somewhat higher mitragynine blood concentrations without any evidence of adverse cardiovascular or any other serious adverse effects. 47. The potential dose of mitragynine that would be likely to substantially contribute to or cause death is not known, but Ms. Moller’s documented level appears to have been very low. Additionally, post-mortem testing identified at least two cannabinoids, diphenhydramine, and promethazine. Of course, novel fentanyl related substances and other substances may have been involved but not tested for. 48. Plaintiff contends that powdered kratom products sold in the United States are far more dangerous than other natural products that are sold over the counter. This is an overly broad statement given the diversity of kratom products and natural products that are sold over the counter (OTC). For example, many products based on natural and botanical ingredients carry serious health and in some cases addiction risks, such as caffeine, yohimbine, kava, and green tea extract. ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE-BASED SUPPORT FOR OPINIONS Opinion 1: Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the U.S., CSA or under the International Drug Control Conventions of the United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the DEA and UNODC that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. 49. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic by nature of its botanical origin, chemical structure or overall pharmacology and thus it is not included in the CSA or any of the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. Nor has it ever been listed as a national drug threat in DEA’s annual National Drug Threat Assessment reports as necessary to meet statutory requirements for CSA Scheduling. Furthermore, kratom does not produce opioid-like respiratory depressant effects or the powerful euphoria that fuels the opioid epidemic. Its primary alkaloid and metabolites that do have some activity similar to opioids are partial agonists, meaning that their strongest effects are weaker than classic opioids (Henningfield et al. 2018, 2022, 2024; Kruegel et al. 2019; Kruegel et al., 2016; Henningfield and Fant, 2016; Varadi et al. 2016). 50. The DEA, NIDA, the U.S. Assistant Secretary for Health, and the WHO’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence all agree with the conclusion that kratom is not an “opioid” and should not be scheduled as such. 51. In recent years, the FDA has been reevaluating its 2017 and 2018 statements that had suggested kratom had narcotic opioid-like effects. The FDA’s stated position as of December 2023 was that it “ha[d] not yet made a determination regarding whether kratom is dangerous.” (United States v.
